The key invariants are: a repository `waythrough` file always wins over built-in defaults; absence of that file should only enable the explicitly supported common servers; unsupported languages must still require configuration; and command discovery/startup errors must remain visible rather than silently selecting another server. Startup remains one bounded process per configured language, so the dominant cost is the language-server process itself; default selection adds only constant-time local matching.

I’m now tracing configuration ownership and tests so the built-ins land at the narrowest layer without changing manager lifecycle behavior.

The existing manager eagerly starts every configured server, so a “list all defaults” fallback would fail in ordinary repositories unless all six binaries were installed. The smallest safe design is therefore project-aware fallback: when the default config path is absent, inspect a bounded set of root marker files, select only matching built-ins, validate them, and start them as usual. If `waythrough.yaml` appears later, the next Waythrough startup loads that file as the complete override—including custom Go startup—without merging hidden defaults.

I’m checking the repository history and issue context for expected server choices and marker conventions before encoding them.

content.text: The performance reviewer found a valid high-impact issue: the first implementation eagerly starts all five built-in servers, so a Go-only repository could trigger five simultaneous workspace indexes. I’m waiting for the other two reviews before changing the design, but this will need a demand-start path for built-ins rather than merely documenting the fixed process count.

All three reviews are back. I’m applying four concrete fixes: demand-start only for built-in servers; an explicit config-source type instead of a negated boolean; strict rejection of empty/unknown configuration; and a real slice-independence assertion. I’ll preserve eager startup for repository files and define “create a file at any point” as taking effect on the next `serve` start, matching the documented lifecycle. The remaining real-server readiness measurement is an acceptance limitation, not something unit tests can honestly resolve.

Because demand-start changes manager concurrency, I’m also applying the project’s critical-systems design skill for that fix. The invariant is single ownership: concurrent first calls may request startup, but exactly one supervisor may spawn/wait on a given server; shutdown must still prevent any later spawn. The extra synchronization work is constant per tool call, and the payoff is reducing default startup from five processes to only those actually requested.
